subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 3-day-old term boy develops lethargy, poor feeding, tachypnea, and vomiting. Arterial blood gas shows respiratory alkalosis, plasma ammonia is 900 micromol/L, organic acids are normal, and citrulline is low. Genetic testing shows a homozygous mutation in the gene encoding N-acetylglutamate synthase, but carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) protein is present in normal amounts on immunoblot.
question: Which of the following best explains the impaired urea cycle in this infant?

options.text: CPS I is competitively inhibited by excess ammonia at its active site
CPS I requires pyridoxal phosphate, which cannot be conjugated to the apoenzyme in this disorder
Loss of N-acetylglutamate lowers CPS I activity by covalently modifying the enzyme
N-acetylglutamate is an essential allosteric activator of CPS I, and its absence reduces enzyme activity despite normal enzyme protein
The enzyme adopts a Michaelis-Menten kinetic profile that cannot respond to substrate

explanation_correct: N-acetylglutamate is synthesized from acetyl-CoA and glutamate by N-acetylglutamate synthase and is an obligatory allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I. Without it, CPS I protein is present but functionally inactive, so carbamoyl phosphate is not formed, ammonia accumulates, and citrulline is low. This contrasts with primary CPS I deficiency, in which the enzyme protein itself is absent or defective.

explanation_incorrect.A: Ammonia is the substrate rather than an active-site competitive inhibitor, and its elevation is a consequence rather than the cause of the block.
explanation_incorrect.B: CPS I does not require pyridoxal phosphate; it requires N-acetylglutamate as an allosteric activator and uses ATP and bicarbonate in the reaction.
explanation_incorrect.C: The activator is noncovalently bound and its absence does not covalently modify the enzyme; activity is regulated by allosteric binding, not by modification.
explanation_incorrect.E: CPS I is normally an allosteric enzyme with a sigmoidal response to its activator, and the loss of activator binding, not an altered kinetic profile, explains the defect.

educationalObjective: N-acetylglutamate is an essential allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, so deficiency of its synthase causes hyperammonemia even when the enzyme protein is present.
